DRIVER'S LICENSE REQUIREMENT IN JOB POSTINGS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jane Doe · Acme Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes a specific restriction that California's Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) places on job postings and applications that state a driver's license is required, and how that restriction -- added to Government Code section 12940 by Senate Bill 1100, effective January 1, 2025 -- relates to Acme Inc.'s consideration of Jane Doe for Marketing Coordinator. Government Code section 12940(q) makes it an unlawful employment practice for a covered employer to include a statement in a job advertisement, posting, application, or other material that an applicant must have a driver's license, unless the employer reasonably expects driving to be one of the job functions for the position and reasonably believes that an alternative form of transportation would not be comparable in travel time or cost. This document states facts about what that statutory provision says and whom it covers; it does not evaluate Acme Inc.'s specific job posting, application materials, or any hiring decision, and it does not determine whether driving is or is not actually a job function of Marketing Coordinator. This document is not itself a job posting, a job application, an offer of employment, or a determination of compliance with the statute described, and it does not tell Acme Inc. or Jane Doe what to do about any particular hiring decision or application material.

THE CORE RESTRICTION ON STATING A DRIVER'S LICENSE IS REQUIRED
Government Code section 12940(q)(1) states the general rule: an employer commits an unlawful employment practice by including a statement in a job advertisement, posting, application, or other material that an applicant must have a driver's license, unless both of two conditions -- described in the clauses below -- are satisfied. The restriction is written as a prohibition on the statement itself, appearing in one of the four listed kinds of material, rather than as a general prohibition on ever requiring driving-related duties of a position.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "For an employer to include a statement in a job advertisement, posting, application, or other material that an applicant must have a driver’s license unless both of the following conditions are satisfied:"
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(q)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code § 12940(q)(1), introductory clause (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only the introductory sentence of section 12940(q)(1); the two conditions that can make such a statement lawful are quoted separately in the two clauses that follow this one, and the statute's list of "alternative form of transportation" examples is quoted in a later clause. The statute's text lists four specific kinds of material -- "job advertisement, posting, application, or other material" -- and this clause does not resolve what falls within the catch-all term "other material" for a communication that is not itself an advertisement, posting, or application, which the statute's text does not define.

FIRST CONDITION: DRIVING MUST BE AN EXPECTED JOB FUNCTION
The first of the two conditions that section 12940(q)(1) requires before a driver's-license statement is lawful is that the employer reasonably expects driving to be one of the job functions for the position. Both conditions described in this document must be satisfied for the driver's-license statement to fall outside the prohibition; this is the first of them.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The employer reasonably expects driving to be one of the job functions for the position."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(q)(1)(A) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code § 12940(q)(1)(A) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  Known gap: The statute's text uses the standard "reasonably expects," but does not itself define what makes an expectation about job functions reasonable, or state what evidence would establish that driving is or is not one of a given position's job functions -- those are fact-specific questions this document does not resolve for any specific position.

SECOND CONDITION: NO COMPARABLE ALTERNATIVE TRANSPORTATION
The second condition section 12940(q)(1) requires is that the employer reasonably believes that satisfying the driving job function using an alternative form of transportation would not be comparable, in travel time or cost to the employer, to having the applicant drive. Both conditions described in this document must be satisfied; this is the second of them, and it is a separate, additional requirement from the first -- an employer that reasonably expects driving to be a job function still does not satisfy section 12940(q)(1) unless it also reasonably believes no comparable alternative exists.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The employer reasonably believes that satisfying the job function described in paragraph (1) using an alternative form of transportation would not be comparable in travel time or cost to the employer."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(q)(1)(B) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code § 12940(q)(1)(B) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  Known gap: The statute's text sets a comparability standard measured by "travel time or cost to the employer," but does not itself state a threshold, formula, or method for measuring when a difference in travel time or cost stops being "comparable" -- that determination is not resolved by the statute's own text. This clause does not address whether cost or time to the applicant, as opposed to cost to the employer, factors into the statutory standard; the statute's text as quoted here refers only to cost "to the employer."

WHAT COUNTS AS AN "ALTERNATIVE FORM OF TRANSPORTATION"
Section 12940(q)(2) defines "alternative form of transportation," the term used in the second condition above, by a non-exhaustive list of examples: using a ride hailing service, using a taxi, carpooling, bicycling, and walking.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "For purposes of this subdivision, “alternative form of transportation” includes, but is not limited to, all
						of the following:"
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(q)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code § 12940(q)(2), introductory clause (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  "Using a ride hailing service."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(q)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code § 12940(q)(2)(A) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  "Using a taxi."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(q)(2)(B) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code § 12940(q)(2)(B) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  "Carpooling."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(q)(2)(C) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code § 12940(q)(2)(C) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  "Bicycling."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(q)(2)(D) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code § 12940(q)(2)(D) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  "Walking."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(q)(2)(E) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code § 12940(q)(2)(E) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  Known gap: The statute's introductory phrase states the list "includes, but is not limited to" the five examples quoted here, so the statute's own text does not foreclose other means of transportation -- such as public transit or a personal vehicle other than the applicant's own car -- from also qualifying, but it does not name any additional example either. The source HTML wraps the introductory sentence across a line break using a literal newline and tab characters between "all" and "of the following:"; that wrapping is reproduced exactly in this clause's first citation's quote field as a verified source-formatting artifact, not an ellipsis or edit.

WHICH EMPLOYERS THE FEHA DEFINITION OF "EMPLOYER" COVERS
FEHA's definitions section, Government Code section 12926(d), states which entities are an "employer" for purposes of FEHA's unlawful-practices provisions, including the driver's-license restriction described above. It states that "employer" includes any person regularly employing five or more persons, or any person acting as an agent of an employer, directly or indirectly, the state or any political or civil subdivision of the state, and cities, and it separately excludes a religious association or corporation not organized for private profit from that definition.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Employer” includes any person regularly employing five or more persons, or any person acting as an agent of an employer, directly or indirectly, the state or any political or civil subdivision of the state, and cities"
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12926(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code § 12926(d), general employer definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12926.)
  "“Employer” does not include a religious association or corporation not organized for private profit."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12926(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code § 12926(d), religious-association exclusion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12926.)
  Known gap: The statute's text does not itself state how the "five or more persons" threshold is counted -- for example, over what time period, in what location, or whether part-time or out-of-state personnel are included -- leaving that computation to sources outside this section's text. This same definitions section, Government Code section 12926(d), is also cited by other documents in this corpus that address other subdivisions of section 12940; it is being independently verified here for use in this document.

ORIGIN AND EFFECTIVE DATE OF THIS RESTRICTION
Subdivision (q) was added to Government Code section 12940 by Senate Bill 1100 during the 2023-2024 legislative session, and the leginfo.legislature.ca.gov official text of the section carries a history note confirming the amendment and its effective date. As enacted, this restriction became operative January 1, 2025.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(Amended by Stats. 2024, Ch. 877, Sec. 1.   (SB 1100)   Effective January 1, 2025.)"
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12940, official history note (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code § 12940, amendment history note (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only the official amendment history note appended to the end of the statutory text on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov; it does not independently describe the bill's legislative history, committee analyses, or Legislative Counsel's Digest, none of which were fetched or verified in this research session. The source HTML renders the history note with three consecutive space characters both before and after the “(SB 1100)” parenthetical; that spacing is reproduced exactly in the quote below as a verified source-formatting artifact of the official leginfo page, not an editing error.

Position: Marketing Coordinator
Date: _______________
